In brief

Parody. "Our travellers reached the rustic hostelry and alighted from their palfreys. [...] A poor house and a bare larder, quotha! 'Tis a merry rogue": after Martin Cunningham, Jack Power, and their Dublin Castle colleague Crofton show up on the horsedrawn "castle car," an extended comedic dialogue describes their entrance into the bar as if they are Shakespearean noblemen looking for food and drink at a country inn after a long day of riding. The narrator of Cyclops has remarked that Crofton, an "orangeman" (i.e., Protestant and pro-British), has been "gallivanting around the country at the king's expense," so the parody plays with the notion that the innkeeper promises the travelers a much better reception once he learns that they are "the king's messengers." In a veritable flood of Shakespearean vocabulary Joyce evokes the Falstaffian miliueu of noblemen slumming in Elizabethan taverns.

At more length

Gifford says that this scene "Parodies the style of late-nineteenth-century versions of medieval romance," and Killeen writes that it is "done in the style of a nineteenth-century historical novel." It would be nice to know which literary works the two men have in mind. They give no hint, but until some such source is identified one may skeptically observe that the parody does not sound much like a prose romance or a novel, consisting almost entirely of dialogue. Five sentences of third-person prose narration briefly set the scene, and a few narrative shreds introduce the speeches—"cried he," "he said," and so forth—but the rest is energetic, idiomatic conversation. Its vocabulary sounds like Shakespeare's—an impression that any concordance will confirm.

Shakespeare often uses the word "travellers" for people journeying far from home. A sentence in Macbeth sees particularly apt: "Now spurs the lated traveller apace / To gain the timely inn." Joyce's three riders accost the innkeeper in the scornful terms that Shakespeare's aristocrats apply to social inferiors. The contemptuous "sirrah" appears in the plays some 150 times, "knave" 232, and "varlet" 27. The word "fellow" is more neutral but is often used in a commanding, patronizing sense. The adjective "saucy"—used, like the modern "uppity," for underlings who are disrespectfully bold or opinionated—appears in the plays 35 times. The parody calls the innkeeper "Mine host", echoing the common expressions "mine host" and "mine hostess" that appear often in plays featuring Falstaff: 2 Henry IV (once), Henry V (2 times), and The Merry Wives of Windsor (20). The innkeeper protests that "my poor house has but a bare larder," using a phrase found in five different plays. But on learning that he is dealing with "The king's friends," a phrase found in 2 Henry VI, or his "messengers," an expression used in King Lear and other plays, he promises to feed them well.

One of the travelers, "a lusty trencherman by his aspect," demands specifics. His cognomen recalls Beatrice's sardonic description of Benedick as "a very valiant trencherman" with "an excellent stomach." In reply, the innkeeper reels off a list of tasty dishes he could furnish. One is "a squab pigeon pasty." Justice Shallow orders "pigeons" for supper in 2 Henry IV, and in Merry Wives Page tells visiting gentlemen that "we have a hot venison pasty to dinner." Some "collops of venison" are also available in the inn, echoing an obscure word in 1 Henry VI and The Winter's Tale that means a bit of meat cut from a larger piece. The "medlar tansy" is a pudding made with medlars, a fruit mentioned half a dozen times in Shakespeare. The list concludes with "a flagon of old Rhenish," whose allusion is quite specific: Hamlet thinks of Rhenish wine twice, including a memory of how Yorick "pour'd a flagon of Rhenish on my head once."

Identifying possible sources of every borrowed word or phrase in this passage would be a tedious undertaking, but it is important to recognize just how pointedly Joyce deploys bardic vocabulary in every sentence. His travelers are said to have "alighted" (a word used in five plays for getting off a horse) from their "palfreys" (smooth-gaited horses), later referred to as "steeds" (strong, high-spirited horses). The inn is "rustic," an adjective that Shakespeare uses several times, and its windows sport the cross-hatched Tudor "lattice" pattern mentioned in several plays. One of the travelers knocks on the window with his "swordhilt," making a Joycean compound word of Shakespeare's many mentions of  sword "hilts." Shakespeare frequently uses "countenance" or "aspect" or "visage" to mean "face" or "facial expression," and "party" to mean "group." The innkeeper's "obsequious" bow carries its neutral Shakespearean meaning of "dutiful, obedient, servile" rather than the negative modern one of "insincerely fawning." He answers a "summons," or order to appear, whose meaning has not changed much over the centuries. His face becomes "overspread" with welcome for the king's men, echoing the King's comment in 2 Henry IV that Hal's princely soil has become "overspread" with weeds.

And then there are the idiomatic expressions, seemingly endless imitations of everyday Elizabethan speech. Instead of exclaiming something, Shakespeare's people are always being said to have "cried" it. They are forever exclaiming "Ho!" They also say, "Cry you mercy" ("I beg your pardon"), "I warrant me" ("I promise"), "Look to" ("pay attention to," "take care of"), "God shield" ("may God protect") and "God bless," and "An you be" ("If you are"). For "anything," they often say "aught." They address their superiors as "good masters" ("gentlemen," "respected sirs") or "your lordships." They wish one another "good den" ("good evening"), and Joyce's "Give you good den" finds an exact analogue in Titus Andronicus when a clown says, "God and Saint Stephen give you good den." After hearing the rich list of foods, the man who asked to see a menu laughs, "A poor house and a bare larder, quotha!" ("said he"). This phrase is usually written "quoth 'a" in Shakespeare's texts, but used in precisely this sarcastic way. A similar orthographical variant occurs when one of the travelers says that "ifaith" ("truly") they need food. The expression pervades Shakespeare's plays, but it is written "in faith," "i' faith," or simply "faith."

In Scylla and Charybdis Joyce notes Shakespeare's preoccupation with gourmandizing abundance: "His art, more than the art of feudalism as Walt Whitman called it, is the art of surfeit. Hot herringpies, green mugs of sack, honeysauces, sugar of roses, marchpane, gooseberried pigeons, ringocandies." That chapter displays extensive knowledge of Shakespeare's works, and in the Cyclops passage Joyce puts his wide reading to use, applying a thick layer of Shakespearean vocabulary to the dialogue. He adds a few small touches of his own, probably thinking that they sound authentic: "Lackaday," "Gadzooks," "his mien," and "hostelry." A "boar's head with pistachios" is his witty addition to the bard's foodstuffs, but it may have been inspired by Posthumus's mention of "a full-acorn'd boar" in Cymbeline. The plays have no "widgeon" (wild duck) served with "crisp hog's bacon," but Falstaff does say in 1 Henry IV that Poins has no more valour than a wild duck.

Two more inventive additions to the Shakespearean vocabulary may be taken as acts of hommage. The innkeeper wears a "tabard," a sleeveless or short-sleeved apron, over his clothes. Shakespeare never used this word in his writings, but he did regularly frequent the Tabard Inn in Southwark, the same inn in which Chaucer's pilgrims spend the night in the Prologue to the Canterbury Tales. In another wonderful touch, this one demonstrating the proverb that imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, Joyce has one of the visitors give the innkeeper a name such as one Shakespeare character might give another: "So servest thou the king's messengers, master Taptun?" The man taps tuns for a living, just as Doll Tearsheet tears sheets in her passion, Pistol threatens bodily harm, and Hotspur hotly spurs his roan steed.

What is one to make of all this? Like many of the parodies, the Shakespeare passage looks back to early modern times, but not in order to mock contemporary Irish glorification of the country's past. This is an English past, and there is nothing glorified about it. Nor does the passage satirize or lampoon anyone, as most other parodies do. Treating the three newcomers as messengers of the King is small potatoes compared to other Cyclopean exaggerations, and quite anodyne. The focus on eating does not exaggerate anything in the present scene—no one in Barney Kiernan's requests, serves, or discusses food. The real spirit of gigantism lives in the flood of Elizabethan words. Joyce has fun with these just as he did with Ireland's fish and produce, the names and physical attributes of great heroes, the astral bodies of Theosophy, the physiological factors leading to ejaculation, the foreign dignitaries at an execution, the euphemisms of parliamentary discourse, the details of a boxing match, the trees in European forests, and the scenes crammed onto a handkerchief. Uproariously excessive cataloguing here is indulged for its own sake.

If there is a rationale for the parody, it must be simply to mock, celebrate, or otherwise engage with Shakespeare. After setting him up in Scylla as the literary competition to beat, here Joyce playfully imitates his dramatic dialogue. It is a preamble to the much more ambitious mimetic rivalry he will undertake in Circe, where narrative entirely disappears.

Joyce's choice of dramatic setting is strange—the Falstaffian tavern scenes are urban, not "rustic," and so is Barney Kiernan's—but evidently he liked the result enough to return to it in Finnegans Wake. In that work's second chapter, one of the first he wrote, HCE comes out of his rural tavern (it is also the Garden of Eden) to greet a very English king (he is also God) who has halted on the turnpike. His Majesty engages the bumpkin, asking him about the flowerpots he carries inverted on poles, and is answered with some rustic dialogue: "Naw, yer maggers, aw war jist a cotchin on thon bluggy earwuggers" (31).

John Hunt 2026
